ap_psychology-m01.set_intro: Researchers studied reading ability in 100 pairs of identical twins and 100 pairs of fraternal twins, all raised together by their families. For each pair, the researchers measured how similar the two twins' reading scores were, using a correlation coefficient. The table shows the results.

options.why: Fraternal twins show a considerable correlation, and identical twins' correlation is not 1.0, so other factors matter.

options.text: Heredity and environment have no influence on reading ability.
options.why: Both correlations are positive and substantial.

options.text: Reading ability is determined entirely by the family environment.
options.why: Identical twins are more similar than fraternal twins, which suggests a role for genes.

options.text: Reading ability appears to be influenced by both heredity and environment.
options.why: The identical twins are more similar than the fraternal twins, which suggests a role for heredity, and the fraternal twins are still similar, which is consistent with shared environment.

ap_psychology-m03.set_intro: A researcher invited 50 volunteers to join a discussion club. Volunteers were randomly assigned to one of two entrance procedures. In the easy procedure, they simply signed a form. In the demanding procedure, they spent an hour completing a long and tedious set of tasks to qualify. Afterward, all volunteers listened to the same dull recording of a club discussion and rated how interesting and valuable the club seemed on a scale from 1 (not at all) to 10 (extremely). The mean rating was 4.1 in the easy group and 6.8 in the demanding group. After the study, the researcher explained the true purpose of the study and the reason for the different entrance procedures.

stimulus.description: Study description (no table or figure accompanies it)

items.stem: Which concept best explains why the demanding-procedure group rated the club higher?

options.text: Social facilitation
options.why: Social facilitation is a change in performance in the presence of others.

options.text: Out-group homogeneity bias
options.why: Out-group homogeneity is seeing members of other groups as alike.

options.text: Mere exposure effect
options.why: The mere exposure effect is increased liking from repeated exposure.

options.text: Cognitive dissonance
options.why: People reduce the discomfort of conflicting actions and attitudes, here by deciding that a club that cost much effort must be worthwhile.

options.why: The data come from an inventory and self-reports rather than observation in a natural setting.

options.text: Meta-analysis of earlier studies
options.why: A meta-analysis combines results of earlier studies rather than collecting new scores.

options.text: Correlational study
options.why: The researcher measures two existing variables and calculates their relationship without manipulation.

options.text: Experiment manipulating conscientiousness
options.why: Conscientiousness is measured, not manipulated, and no one is randomly assigned.

ap_psychology-m07.stem: Researchers randomly assign 100 volunteers to write about their personal strengths or about a neutral topic, and then measure each volunteer's self-efficacy with a questionnaire. Which research design is this?

options.text: Naturalistic observation in an ordinary setting
options.why: Participants were assigned a task; behavior was not simply observed in a natural setting.

options.text: Experiment with random assignment
options.why: The researchers manipulate the writing task and randomly assign participants.

options.text: Survey, as participants answered questions
options.why: A survey does not manipulate a variable or randomly assign participants.

options.text: Correlational study, as a questionnaire was used
options.why: Using a questionnaire does not make a study correlational when a variable is manipulated with random assignment.

ap_psychology-m08.stem: A positive-psychology study finds that a gratitude exercise raises well-being. Three independent labs repeat the procedure with new participants and find no effect. What is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.text: Replications count only if the original researchers run them.
options.why: Independent replication is valuable precisely because it is run by others.

options.text: The original study must have been unethical.
options.why: Failure to replicate says nothing about whether a study was ethical.

options.text: The failed replications prove that gratitude lowers well-being.
options.why: No effect is not evidence of a harmful effect.

options.text: The original finding is less certain and needs further testing.
options.why: Conclusions evolve through replication; failed replications reduce confidence in the original result.

ap_psychology-m08.stem: Which feature of peer review best helps prevent weak research from being published?

options.text: The journal publishes only studies with statistically significant results.
options.why: Publishing only significant results creates bias rather than preventing weak research.

options.text: Study participants vote on whether the study should be published.
options.why: Participants are not the evaluators in peer review.

options.text: The authors choose which reviewers evaluate their own work.
options.why: Authors choosing their own reviewers would weaken, not strengthen, the check.

options.text: Independent experts evaluate the methods and conclusions before publication.
options.why: Peer review is evaluation of research by other scientists before publication.

options.text: Correlational data, because the researcher compared two variables

options.text: Qualitative data
options.why: Open-ended descriptive responses grouped into themes are qualitative.

options.text: Experimental data, because the researcher interacted with the athletes
options.why: Interviewing is not manipulating a variable.

options.text: Quantitative data, because the answers were grouped into categories
options.why: Grouping answers into themes does not turn descriptive responses into numerical scores.

ap_psychology-m09.stem: Which survey item is most likely to produce a leading-question or social desirability bias?

options.text: On a scale from 1 to 5, how motivated do you feel today?
options.why: A rating scale with neutral wording is not leading.

options.text: Most experts agree that rewards ruin motivation, don't you?
options.why: The wording signals the expected answer and pressures respondents to agree.

options.text: What is the main reason you practice?
options.why: An open question does not suggest an answer.

options.text: How many hours did you practice last week?
options.why: This asks for a factual number without signaling an expected answer.

ap_psychology-m10.stem: In a trial of a new therapy for panic attacks, participants are told they might be placed on a waiting list, that they can leave at any time, and that their records will be identified only by codes. Which pair of ethical guidelines is being applied?

options.text: Random assignment and double-blind procedure
options.why: These are design techniques rather than ethical guidelines.

options.text: Operational definition and replication
options.why: These are scientific concepts rather than ethical guidelines.

options.text: Informed consent and confidentiality
options.why: Participants agreed knowing the procedures and right to withdraw, and their identities were protected.

options.text: Debriefing and deception
options.why: Nothing in the description involves misleading participants or explaining a hidden purpose afterward.

ap_psychology-m10.stem: Halfway through a therapy trial, a clinician sees that several participants in the treatment group are getting worse. Which action best follows ethical principles?

options.text: Keep the observation private until the results are published.
options.why: Withholding a known risk from participants and the review board is not ethical.

options.text: Stop or modify the procedure to protect participants from harm.
options.why: Researchers must take steps to protect participants from harm.

options.text: Finish data collection so that the study results stay valid.
options.why: Participants' welfare takes precedence over data collection.

options.text: Stop telling participants about the risks so that fewer of them drop out.
options.why: Participants must be kept informed of risks.

ap_psychology-m11.stem: In a trial of a new antidepressant, participants are randomly assigned to receive the drug or an identical-looking pill with no active ingredient. Neither the participants nor the staff who measure symptoms know who received which pill. Which pair of terms describes the design?

options.text: Placebo control group and single-blind procedure
options.why: Both participants and staff are unaware, so the procedure is double-blind.

options.text: Experimental group and open-label procedure
options.why: An open-label procedure would tell everyone who received the drug.

options.text: Placebo control group and double-blind procedure
options.why: An inactive pill gives a comparison, and keeping both participants and assessors unaware controls expectations and experimenter bias.

options.text: Waiting-list control group and single-blind procedure
options.why: No one is placed on a waiting list, and both participants and staff are blind.

ap_psychology-m11.stem: A researcher wants to know whether improvement after therapy comes from the therapy itself or from clients' expectation of getting help. Which design element best addresses this question?

options.text: A case study of one client
options.why: A single case cannot separate treatment effects from expectation.

options.text: A satisfaction survey after the study
options.why: Satisfaction ratings cannot separate real improvement from expectation.

options.text: A larger sample from a single clinic
options.why: A larger sample does not separate treatment from expectation.

options.text: A comparison group that receives an inactive treatment
options.why: A placebo-style comparison separates the effect of the treatment from the effect of expectations.
